clinicalPearls: Defined in young children by severe wasting (weight-for-height well below the reference median, or a very low mid-upper arm circumference) and/or bilateral pitting oedema of nutritional origin.
Marasmus is severe wasting from overall energy deficit; kwashiorkor is characterised by oedema, and mixed pictures occur.
Kwashiorkor features include oedema, sparse depigmented hair, skin changes (flaky-paint dermatosis), an enlarged fatty liver, and apathy.
Children with SAM are highly vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and overwhelming infection, which is often present without classic signs.
Refeeding must be cautious and staged to avoid refeeding syndrome; overly rapid feeding and excess fluid or sodium can precipitate cardiac failure and death.
Initial stabilisation prioritises treating and preventing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, correcting dehydration carefully, and giving broad micronutrient support.
Rehydration is preferably oral or nasogastric with a low-sodium, higher-potassium solution, because intravenous fluids readily cause fluid overload.
Management follows a stabilisation phase with cautious feeding, followed by a rehabilitation phase with catch-up growth once appetite and stability return.
reference.pathophysiology: Prolonged inadequate intake of energy, protein, and micronutrients forces the body into a state of reductive adaptation: metabolic rate falls, organ function is downregulated, and body composition shifts with loss of fat and muscle. Sodium-potassium pump activity is impaired, causing intracellular sodium retention and total-body potassium and magnesium depletion despite oedema. Hepatic and cardiac function, immune competence, and thermoregulation are all compromised. In kwashiorkor, hypoalbuminaemia and increased capillary permeability contribute to oedema. These adaptations make the child dangerously intolerant of the metabolic demands of aggressive feeding and fluid loads.
additionalDifferentials: Oedema from nephrotic syndrome or cardiac/hepatic failure
Malabsorption syndromes (e.g. coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis)
Underlying malignancy or chronic illness causing wasting
additionalInvestigations: Weight, height/length, and mid-upper arm circumference with oedema assessment
Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, and phosphate
Screening for infection (including tuberculosis, HIV where relevant) and malaria in endemic areas
Assessment of hydration status, which is difficult to judge clinically in SAM
redFlags: Signs of shock or severe dehydration (difficult to assess and easy to overtreat)
Developing signs of heart failure during rehydration or refeeding (refeeding syndrome)
Lethargy, hypothermia, or hypoglycaemia as subtle markers of serious infection
reference.prognosis: With careful phased management and treatment of complications, most children recover, but case fatality is high when complications such as hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, sepsis, or refeeding syndrome are missed or when rehydration is too aggressive.
pitfalls: Feeding too much too quickly and precipitating refeeding syndrome and heart failure
Using standard intravenous rehydration and causing fluid overload
Relying on usual signs of infection, which are often absent
Missing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia because signs are subtle
Treating oedema as fluid overload rather than recognising nutritional kwashiorkor
management: Cautious, staged refeeding starting with a low-protein starter therapeutic milk and transitioning to catch-up feed or ready-to-use therapeutic food to avoid refeeding syndrome
Prevent and treat hypoglycaemia and hypothermia with frequent feeds and active warming
Correct dehydration cautiously with a low-sodium oral rehydration solution, reserving intravenous fluids for shock
Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics because infection is common and often occult
Correct electrolyte and micronutrient deficits with potassium, magnesium, zinc, and multivitamins, withholding iron until the recovery phase
Monitor for and manage complications including cardiac failure, sepsis, and refeeding syndrome
Structured nutritional rehabilitation, developmental stimulation, and caregiver education with community follow-up
Manage within a paediatric nutrition multidisciplinary programme
